criteria_quotes:
Aetna considers total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a Food and Drug Administration-cleared implant (e.g., the Agility LP Total Ankle, the Eclipse Total Ankle, the INBONE Total Ankle, the Infinity Total Ankle System, the STAR system, the Salto Talaris Total Ankle Prosthesis, and the Zimmer Trabecular Metal Total Ankle) medically necessary when the following criteria are met:
TAA is used to replace an arthritic or severely degenerated ankle; and
Member is skeletally mature; and
Member has with moderate or severe pain with loss of ankle mobility and function; and
Imaging is consistent with severe arthritis / degeneration of the ankle due to osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis), post-traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis; and
Member has have failed at least 6 months of conservative management (including physical therapy* by a licensed physical therapist, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and orthoses as indicated); and
If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to surgery; and
Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below

Physical therapy (in-person as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) must be recent (within the past year), for at least 6 weeks (12 weeks with age less than 50 years or BMI greater than 40), and needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate and not required for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint.

Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below:
Absence of the medial or lateral malleolus
Active or prior deep infection in the ankle joint or adjacent bones
Avascular necrosis of the talus
Charcot joint
Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty
Hindfoot or forefoot mal-alignment precluding plantigrade foot
Insufficient bone or musculature such that proper component positioning or alignment is not possible
Insufficient ligament support that can not be repaired with soft tissue stabilization
Lower extremity vascular insufficiency
Neuromuscular disease resulting in lack of normal muscle function about the affected ankle
Osteonecrosis
Peripheral neuropathy (may lead to Charcot joint of the affected ankle)
Poor skin and soft tissue quality about the surgical site
Prior arthrodesis (fusion) at the ankle joint
Prior surgery or injury that has adversely affected ankle bone quality
Psychiatric problems that hinder adequate cooperation during peri-operative period
Severe anatomic deformity in adjacent ankle structures, including hindfoot, forefoot and knee joint
Severe ankle deformity (e.g., severe varus or valgus deformity) that would not normally be eligible for ankle arthroplasty
Severe osteoporosis, osteopenia or other conditions resulting in poor bone quality, as this may result in inadequate bony fixation
Significant mal-alignment of the knee joint
Skeletal maturity not yet reached
Vascular insufficiency in the affected limb.
